Testing symmetry too — checking whether shapes are invariant under 180-degree rotation, since that could be the distinguishing property instead of cell count or duplicates.

I also check proximity to the grid center and enclosed background cells, but neither seems to explain why a shape gets picked, so I keep looking for symmetry or another structural clue.

I check symmetry axes across ex1 shapes: 8 has top-bottom mirror symmetry while 1 and 5 have vertical-axis symmetry instead, so multiple shapes qualify as symmetric but 8 stands out as the only horizontally symmetric one. Testing this idea on ex2's answer, shape 2 doesn't show clear left-right or top-bottom symmetry either, so I start checking the symmetry of ex2's other shapes to see if the pattern still holds.

Since none of ex2's shapes turn out symmetric, this rules out symmetry as the deciding factor. I try other angles instead: matching bounding box shape, row count, or area, but none of these distinguish the correct answer consistently across examples. I then consider treating the shapes as paths and counting endpoints, noticing that ex1's answer 8 and ex3's answer 6 both look like path shapes with exactly two endpoints, which seems promising.

Next I wonder if the target shape is a scaled or extended version of a smaller shape present elsewhere in the same grid—in ex3, shape 6 looks like shape 7 with extended arms, though the scaling isn't exact. I try applying similar reasoning to ex1's shape 8 but can't find a matching smaller shape, so I move on to consider whether the answer might instead correlate with the shape's color value being the largest among those present.

That doesn't hold either—ex2's answer is color 2, which is actually the smallest value, not largest, and ex3's answer 6 isn't extreme in either direction. I also test whether the answer always touches the leftmost column, but ex3 breaks that pattern since shape 5 is at column 0 while the actual answer is 6. Position within the grid doesn't show an obvious consistent rule either, since the answers land in different regions across examples (bottom-left, top-left, bottom-middle), so I start reconsidering whether cell count might be the deciding factor after all.

Now I'm checking if a duplicate shape topology explains the answer—comparing whether shape 8's outline matches another shape like 3 or 7 cell-for-cell, but they don't line up when I trace their cell patterns. I also try comparing cell count against bounding box perimeter for shape 8, and consider counting holes or enclosed regions as another possible distinguishing feature.

Let me try density: filled cells divided by bounding box area for each shape. In example 2, shape 2 has the highest density at 0.8, matching the answer, and in example 3, shape 6 doesn't have the highest density (7 and 5 tie at 0.75), so this rule doesn't hold consistently and I need another approach.

I'm also revisiting example 1's shape 6 layout to double-check I've read the rows correctly, and considering whether the answer relates to symmetric L-shapes or corner shapes instead.

Let me try another angle: maybe the target shape is the one that's structurally unique while the rest come in congruent pairs under rotation. Comparing shapes 2 and 8, and then 3 and 4 in example 2, checking if their cell counts and arm lengths match up as rotated duplicates.

Since that's not panning out, I'm wondering if the count of shapes equals the answer's cell count, but that only fits example 3. I'm also considering bounding box area as a distinguishing feature, but that doesn't cleanly separate the target from the rest either.

Now I'm testing whether the selected shape is defined by having both a straight horizontal and vertical run of length 3 in its outline, checking each example's shapes against that, and also toying with the idea that the longest contiguous line segment across the grid picks out the answer.

But that fails on example 1, so I'm second-guessing and instead counting exact cell positions for each shape, wondering if the criterion is really about enclosed pockets or concavities within the bounding box rather than raw cell counts or line lengths.

That doesn't match either. I checked transpose symmetry across examples—the 6 shape in ex3 turned out symmetric across its diagonal, but the others didn't, and shapes aren't even square in some cases. Let me try another angle for what distinguishes the selected shape.

I'm testing whether the odd-one-out contains a 2x2 block of filled cells, but that split doesn't cleanly separate the shapes either—some non-selected shapes have 2x2 blocks and some don't. Now I'm checking whether the distinguishing feature is a branching cell with three or more neighbors instead.

Checking each shape against this rule shows some pass trivially due to thin bounding boxes, while others fail when an interior cell is actually filled, so this criterion isn't clean either.

Maybe I'm overanalyzing the border/interior angle. I consider whether the answer is simply the shape with the most cells, and start rechecking cell counts per shape in example 3.

Recounting example 3's rows gives a total of 7 cells, more than 5, so cell count doesn't seem to determine the answer either. I try another angle: maybe the answer avoids 2x2 blocks entirely, but example 2's answer shape actually has an 8-cell region including a 2x2 block, so that idea also fails.

I move to checking whether bounding box dimensions are unique across shapes, then try counting corners along each shape's outline path, tracing through the coordinates to see if a distinct corner count sets the answer apart.

Then I try ordering shapes by reading order (first appearance by row/column) and check whether the answer is always the k-th shape in that sequence, testing this against multiple examples.

But the results are inconsistent — 3rd in one, 1st in another, 5th in another — so that ordering theory doesn't hold up.

Then I notice a possible coincidence: the winning shape in one example looks structurally like the winning shape in another example, just with an extra row, which makes me wonder if shape similarity across puzzles matters rather than position.

I try counting cells per shape to see if odd/even parity or max-count breaks ties, but ties keep appearing between different-colored shapes, so I move to trying perimeter as a discriminator, computing cells and internal adjacencies for each shape to get 4×cells − 2×adjacencies.

Still no shape stands out uniquely though — several come out with matching perimeters, so I start wondering if the answer instead depends on shape topology, like whether one forms a closed loop or hook whose cell count matches the number of other shapes present.

I try counting zeros inside bounding boxes, but that doesn't match either. Maybe the rule is about largest or smallest square bounding box among shapes — testing that against the examples, but neither largest nor smallest consistently picks the right answer.

I check whether the answer shape is symmetric under transpose or anti-diagonal reflection, computing the transpose of shape 8 in example 1 and finding it doesn't match, so that symmetry idea fails too.

Then I try color parity: shape 8 and 6 are both even, but shape 2's color set doesn't fit that pattern cleanly either, so evenness alone isn't the rule. I go back to considering whether the answer relates to which shape has the largest row or column of filled cells.

Testing height as the distinguishing feature: in example 2, shape 2 stands taller than shapes 8, 3, and 4, and in example 1, shape 7 has the greatest height among all the pieces—so maximum height might actually be the deciding factor.

Now I'm checking cell counts for the bounding boxes instead—comparing shape sizes against their perimeters didn't line up either. Trying another angle: maybe the correct shape is the one whose cell count doesn't match any other shape's count, though checking example 1's counts against colors doesn't quite confirm this either.

Counting cells for colors 5 and 6 gives 4 each, and I'm checking whether their shapes are congruent under rotation—5 looks like a T-tetromino while 6 looks like a J/L tetromino, so they're different pieces despite matching counts. That leaves colors 3, 7, and 8 all tied at 7 cells each.

Trying another angle, I check whether shapes 3 and 4 in example 2 (both 6 cells) are congruent by comparing their cell layouts—3 is an L-shape with a long horizontal arm while 4 is a rotated U-shape, so they don't match either. Same story for 2 versus 8 at 8 cells each—not congruent. Maybe the rule isn't about matching pairs of shapes but something like largest bounding box, though that doesn't hold up well against example 3, so I want to re-verify my grid parsing for example 3 to make sure I haven't misassigned any cells to the wrong shape.

Recounting the shapes, I get sizes 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 with answer 6 (5 cells)—the exact median. In example 1, sizes 4,4,7,7,7,8 give a median of 7 with three tied candidates, and the answer 8 is among them. In example 2, sizes 6,6,8,8 split evenly around 7, and the answer is 8. So there's a rough median pattern, but the tie-breaking logic isn't clear yet—example 1 picks the largest among ties (8) while example 2's winner (2, at 8 cells) doesn't fit that same logic cleanly. This feels too weak, so I want to search for a more consistent measure across all three examples.

I try bbox emptiness, area, and width as candidates, but none give a unique winner without ties across examples. Maybe the key is counting straight-line strokes needed to draw each shape—like treating each shape as a sequence of maximal horizontal and vertical runs, similar to how many pen strokes it'd take to draw the letter C.

I'm trying other properties like duplicate shapes or symmetry, none quite fitting. Then I try grouping shapes by spatial region in the grid — checking which rows each shape occupies and noticing the answer tends to be the leftmost or a specific member within a cluster of shapes in one region.

Now I'm testing a distance-to-corner idea, calculating rough coordinates for shapes near the bottom-left corner in one example to see if the answer shape is simply closest to it, but the distances come out tied.

Let me instead try counting endpoint cells — cells with exactly one neighbor — for each shape, tallying up how many endpoints each shape has across the examples to see if that count distinguishes the answer shape.

Checking the rest: examples 7, 5, 1 all trace out as simple paths with 2 endpoints. Then region 9 with its scattered cells also traces into one continuous path connecting endpoints (5,3) and (4,6) - so it turns out every example is just a path shape.

Their lengths are 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 respectively, and the answer picks length 6, which matches the median again - so that pattern doesn't distinguish anything new.

But then in example 2, one of the shapes has 8 cells forming a 2x2 block, so it isn't a simple path at all, yet the answer for that example is a different shape entirely, not a path. That breaks my "always pick the path" theory, so I need to look for another distinguishing feature - maybe something about symmetry or a spiral shape - but sketching out that 8-cell shape doesn't look like a spiral either. I'm now considering whether the rule is about matching cell counts between shapes instead.

Both the 2-colored and 8-colored shapes have exactly 8 cells each, yet the answer is the 2-shape, so maybe bounding box size or density is the tiebreaker - the 2-shape has a bounding box of 10 while the 8-shape has 12, meaning the 2-shape is denser despite being taller and narrower. Testing this against example 1, though, the shape with the most cells (8 total, from the 1-colored region) isn't the answer, so density or cell-count maximization doesn't hold universally either.

Maybe border-touching disqualifies shapes, since the 1-shape in example 1 touches the bottom row - but the 8-shape in example 2 touches the left border too, so that theory breaks down as well. I'm also considering whether mirror symmetry could be the deciding factor, but checking the 2-shape's structure shows no such symmetry, so that's ruled out too. Perhaps the real pattern involves two shapes sharing the same form but at different scales - checking whether the 4-shape's U-shape appears elsewhere in a rotated or resized form.

Let me check congruences directly across example 1's shapes—normalizing each and comparing rotations. None of them turn out to be congruent pairs, so that symmetry idea doesn't hold up. I'm now wondering if the target shapes share some other structural trait, like matching line lengths at both ends.

Trying a different angle: maybe the answer relates to overall shape counts or grid dimensions in each example, but the numbers don't line up cleanly either. I'm now testing whether the target shape is the one containing both a horizontal and vertical line segment of length three, checking whether that holds for example 1's shape C.

Trying counting straight lines of length ≥3 per shape: in example 1, C has three such lines while others have one or two, so C wins clearly. But testing this on example 3, both 6 and 9 tie with two lines each, so this rule doesn't cleanly resolve every case either.
